raw_text:
The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) has emerged as a revolutionary therapeutic standard for the prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD). Conventional transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (TV-ICDs) carry inherent risks due to endovascular lead placement, including acute complications like pneumothorax or cardiac perforation, and long-term issues like lead fracture, venous occlusion, tricuspid regurgitation, and systemic endocarditis. To mitigate these risks, the S-ICD was designed to be implanted entirely extra-thoracically, utilizing a parasternal lead and a mid-axillary pulse generator. This breakthrough system was first introduced in 2010 by Bardy et al. [1]. Subsequent regulatory approval was supported by the United States Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) trial, which demonstrated high conversion rates for induced ventricular fibrillation (VF) and confirmed early safety [2].

Following clinical adoption, the performance of the S-ICD was tracked in large-scale clinical registries. The international EFFORTLESS registry demonstrated low perioperative complication rates [3], and its five-year follow-up confirmed robust, sustained protection, showing a 98.2% discrete VF conversion rate and zero structural lead failures [4]. Concurrently, the US S-ICD Post-Approval Study (PAS) validated this favorable safety profile in clinical practice [5], showing high long-term system integrity and low infection rates at three years [6].

Robust randomized controlled trial (RCT) evidence has solidified the role of S-ICD therapy. The head-to-head PRAETORIAN trial showed that the S-ICD is non-inferior to the TV-ICD regarding the primary composite endpoint of inappropriate shocks and device-related complications [7]. Crucially, S-ICD recipients experienced significantly fewer lead-related complications over a median follow-up of 49 months. The ATLAS trial reinforced these findings, demonstrating a 92% reduction in major lead-related complications during early follow-up [8]. Furthermore, the UNTOUCHED trial evaluated S-ICD outcomes in a classic primary prevention cohort with severe left ventricular dysfunction; using standardized high-rate programming and contemporary filtering algorithms, the eighteen-month inappropriate shock-free rate was 95.9% [9].

Reflecting this evidence, international clinical guidelines from the AHA/ACC/HRS recommend S-ICD as a Class I therapy for patients with difficult venous access or high infection risk, and a Class IIa therapy for those requiring an ICD without pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), or antitachycardia pacing (ATP) indications [10]. The ESC guidelines provide similar class endorsements [11]. In cases where pocket or lead complications occur, specialized surgical management protocols can optimize outcomes [12].

Because the S-ICD relies on subcutaneous electrograms, inappropriate shocks (IAS) due to oversensing of T-waves or skeletal myopotentials remain a clinical focus. Advanced software features, such as the SMART-Pass filter, have significantly reduced IAS rates by attenuating low-frequency noise without compromising VF detection [13]. To ensure sensing fidelity, pre-implantation electrocardiographic screening is mandatory to evaluate the patient's QRS-T wave morphology [14]. This screening process has shown high eligibility rates, particularly in specific cohorts at high risk for endovascular lead failure, such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) [15].

Surgical techniques have also evolved to improve safety and patient comfort. While early S-ICD implants utilized a three-incision technique, a simpler two-incision technique was introduced by Knops et al., which eliminates the superior parasternal incision and enhances cosmesis [16]. Generator placement has also transitioned from a subcutaneous pocket to an intermuscular space beneath the latissimus dorsi, reducing skin erosion, device discomfort, and chronic pain [17].

Historically, the primary limitation of S-ICD therapy has been its inability to deliver bradycardia pacing or ATP. To resolve this, modular cardiac rhythm management (mCRM) systems have been developed, linking the S-ICD with a wirelessly communicating leadless pacemaker [18]. Preclinical and early clinical proof-of-concept studies demonstrated the feasibility of this communicating configuration [19]. In the landmark 2024 MODULAR ATP trial, Knops et al. demonstrated that this wirelessly communicating modular pacing-defibrillator system safely and effectively delivers ATP and bradycardia pacing, successfully overcoming S-ICD's traditional pacing limitation [18].

To optimize clinical workflow, researchers designed the randomized PRAETORIAN-DFT trial to evaluate whether routine intraoperative defibrillation testing (DFT) can be safely omitted [20]. Understanding the incidence and predictors of inappropriate shocks remains key to refining S-ICD sensing [21]. Implant positioning can be systematically assessed using the post-operative radiographic PRAETORIAN score, which strongly predicts DFT success [22]. Long-term device replacement procedures have shown low complication rates [23]. Pre-implantation screening failure remains a challenge, as failed QRS-T wave screening can exclude a subset of candidates [24]. In pediatric and young adult populations, registries such as the SIDECAR project have confirmed S-ICD safety and efficacy, highlighting its utility in younger cohorts with long life expectancies [25]. The shift toward omitting routine DFT in S-ICDs was informed by transvenous studies, such as the SIMPLE [26] and NORDIC ICD [27] trials, which confirmed that routine DFT does not improve clinical shock success. In primary prevention populations, detailed clinical and perioperative outcomes have been outlined in the baseline analysis of the UNTOUCHED study [28]. Finally, long-term registries have shown similar survival rates and fewer systemic complications with S-ICDs compared to TV-ICDs [29], and they serve as an invaluable replacement therapy following transvenous lead extraction for systemic infection [30].
